name: Carlos Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is kept confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager for the Hartley brothers, Simon and Mark, on about 400 hectares. The main business is an outdoor pig unit, 250 sows in fields with little huts, and we grow wheat, maize and oilseed rape. I start at half six with a walk round the sow paddocks with Dev, my head stockman, then plan the day for the five staff. Afternoons I'm often on the combine or the phone to the feed mill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy a good farrowing week, when the piglet numbers come in high and the sows are content in the mud. What wears me out is the pig price, it goes up and down like a fairground ride, and the brothers ask me why every time. I've done this twenty-six years and I'm proud I'm still the one they call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a few handy tools and lots of noise. At the pig producers' meeting I'd tell people to use what saves time and ignore the rest. I might post something dry about it on the farming forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I've got a steady job, the brothers trust me, and the pig price is the same headache it always was. A pig price crash worries me more than any computer, because the Hartley brothers feel it first and I feel it a month later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep using the AI assistant now and then to check feed contracts, which I started last year. Abena and I would keep putting 200 a month aside, we've got about five months saved. I'd start planning my own retirement around 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Life as normal, with the usual pig price grumbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the pig price crashed in the next couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut back on new huts and hold off hiring, and the brothers might sell some sows. My job would be safe, because someone has to run the place, but a pay rise wouldn't happen. We've ridden out three crashes since 2000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned retirement at 66. Is there a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Abena has a decent school pension, mine is smaller, and we've nearly paid off the house. The plan is to downsize to a bungalow near Esi, our daughter, and help with the grandchildren. Nothing fancy.

say: It's what I expected: a few **handy tools** and lots of noise.
Use what **saves time** and ignore the rest.
I'd post something **dry** about it on the farming forum.
think: I'd be **fine**, with a steady job and owners who trust me.
A **pig price crash** worries me more than any computer.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** now and then to check feed contracts.
Keep saving **200 a month** toward the five-month cushion.
Plan **retirement at 66** with a bungalow near Esi.
S0.quote: A pig price crash worries me more than any computer, because the Hartley brothers feel it first and I feel it a month later.
fieldNote: His one real pressure is the **pig price cycle**, which he has survived before.
He's a **moderate AI user**, already checking contracts with it.
His retirement plan is **concrete and modest**, centred on family.

steps.text: Keep managing the 250-sow outdoor pig unit as now
Keep checking feed contracts with the AI assistant
Save 200 a month toward retirement at 66

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change, but one we can manage if we're sensible. At the producers' meeting I'd say watch the farms that try it first and copy what works. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, part of my job is exactly the thinking stuff: planning rotations, buying feed, writing up records for the inspector. If software does my planning and buying, the Hartley brothers could ask why they pay a manager instead of a head stockman. I don't think they would, but the thought would nag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once two or three neighbours have proven it, I'd get the farm planning software in, maybe in the second year. I'd go on a one-day course at the agricultural college to learn it properly. I'd also make sure the brothers see I'm the one making the software pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just alert, like when the wind turns before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy in the office, who does the records and invoices three days a week. That's the work the software eats first. I'd try to get her trained on the pig side, she's good with animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to prove it. Why not move first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen plenty of farmers buy shiny things that broke in a year. Let someone else find the bugs. I'm happy to be the second one through the gate.

say: It's a **change we can manage** if we're sensible.
Watch the **first farms** to try it and copy what works.
There's no need to **make a fuss** online.
think: My **planning and buying** work is exactly what the software takes.
The owners might ask why they pay a **manager** at all.
do: Bring in **farm planning software** in year two, once neighbours prove it.
Take a **one-day course** at the agricultural college.
Show the brothers he's the one **making it pay**.
feel: **Uneasy** and alert, like the wind **turning** before a storm.
S1.quote: If software does my planning and buying, the Hartley brothers could ask why they pay a manager instead of a head stockman.
fieldNote: He recognises the **thinking part** of his manager role is exposed.
Classic **second-mover**: waits for proof, then adopts properly.
He worries for **Lucy in the office**, whose records work goes first.

steps.text: Buy farm planning software in year two after neighbours try it
Take a one-day course on the software at the agricultural college
Keep Lucy employed by moving her from records onto the pig unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not farmers, not the government, not the banks. At the producers' meeting I'd say we need to stick together and talk to the buyers. To friends I'd just say it's a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the planning and buying half of my job is gone by 2028, and the brothers would need a stockman more than a manager. Robots for pigs in muddy fields come around 2031, when I'm 63. Three years of being a well-paid stockman, then nothing, is not how I pictured finishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask Simon and Mark for a plain talk about my job and a written agreement to 2031. Abena and I would stop the extra mortgage payments and keep that cash as savings instead. I'd also look at what the pension pays at 63, and whether I can bring retirement forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops a bit just thinking about telling Abena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between the thinking AI in 2028 and the robots in 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my boots but lose my desk. For three years I'm useful for the hands-on work, moving sows and fixing fences. Then, if the robots can handle mud and pigs, that's over too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Abena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'll be fine on her pension and our savings if we're careful. Then I'd tell her we might need to sell the house earlier than planned. Abena would want a spreadsheet, so I'd make one.

say: **Nobody's ready**: not farmers, government or banks.
Producers must **stick together** and talk to the buyers.
To friends I'd simply say it's a **mess**.
think: My **planning and buying** work is gone by 2028.
Robots for **pigs in mud** arrive around 2031, when I'm 63.
do: Ask the brothers for a **written agreement** to 2031.
Stop **extra mortgage payments** and hold the cash as savings.
feel: **Anxious**, with a sinking stomach at the thought of **telling Abena**.
S2.quote: Three years of being a well-paid stockman, then nothing, is not how I pictured finishing.
fieldNote: He describes the gap clearly: keeps his **boots**, loses his **desk**.
He moves quickly to **protect cash**, reversing his mortgage plan.
He expects a **downgrade then exit**, not instant job loss.

steps.text: Ask Simon and Mark for a written job agreement to 2031
Stop extra mortgage payments and keep the cash as savings
Check the pension figures for retiring at 63 instead of 66

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's not waste it. At the producers' meeting I'd push for a joint deal on robots, so small farms aren't left behind. I'd tell friends to talk to their bosses early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's tight. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the robots come for the pigs. With five years warning, my plan is to be the manager who runs the robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years I'd learn the planning software fully, once it's proven on a couple of farms. By 2030 I'd be telling the brothers which robots to buy and how to run them. Meanwhile we'd keep saving 200 a month and finish paying off the house by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan in my pocket. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk the brothers sell the farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is. Simon's son isn't interested in farming, and a big investor could offer them good money for a robot-ready farm. If they sold, I'd be 64 and looking, which is a bad spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if they did sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the new owners to keep me on for the switchover, a year or two. After that I'd take the pension early and help Esi with the grandkids. We'd manage, just not in style.

say: There's **time to get ready**, so let's not waste it.
Small farms need a **joint deal** on robots.
think: It's **tight**: 63 for the AI and 66 for the robots.
My aim is to **run the robots**, not be replaced by them.
do: Learn the **planning software** fully in two years.
Advise the brothers on **which robots** to buy by 2030.
S3.quote: With five years warning, my plan is to be the manager who runs the robots, not the one they replace.
fieldNote: He uses the warning time to **reposition** as the robot manager.
A **sale to investors** is the risk he can't control.
His fallback is **early pension** and family care, modest but real.

steps.text: Learn the farm planning software fully within two years
Advise the Hartleys on which pig robots to buy by 2030
Finish paying off the house by 2029
Push the producers' group for a joint robot deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so planning is everyone's own job now. At the producers' meeting I'd say start training youngsters on the robot side. I wouldn't be out campaigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'll be retired before it touches me. I'm 68 for the AI and 71 for the robots, and I stop at 66. My son Kofi will be in the middle of it, and I'd rather it was me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on to 66 as planned. I'd train Dev, my head stockman, to take over as manager and learn whatever new systems come. We'd keep saving and move to the bungalow near Esi in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Kofi and Dev, fine for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi, your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi's an engineer working abroad, designing water systems. I'd tell him to make sure he's the one checking the AI's work, not the one it replaces. He'd probably tell me he's already doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the Hartleys keep the pigs in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if robots make outdoor pigs cheaper. Or they'd move indoors, which I'd hate. I'd have retired, so it wouldn't be my call.

say: Ten years is **plenty**; planning is everyone's own job.
Producers should **train youngsters** on the robot side.
I wouldn't be out **campaigning** about it.
think: I'll be **retired** before it touches me.
My son **Kofi** will be in the middle of it, and I'd rather it was me.
do: Train **Dev** to take over as manager.
Move to the **bungalow near Esi** in 2034.
feel: **Fine** for himself, **uneasy** for Kofi and Dev.
S4.quote: My son Kofi will be in the middle of it, and I'd rather it was me.
fieldNote: The decade turns his worry toward his **son and successor**.
He plans a clean **handover to Dev**, a sign of loyalty to the team.
He dislikes the idea of pigs moving **indoors**, a values point.

steps.text: Keep managing the pig unit until retiring at 66
Train Dev the head stockman to take over as manager
Move to a bungalow near daughter Esi in 2034

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be a stockman at 60 and out at 63. What would help is an agreed way for older managers to step down gently, part-time with a top-up, rather than a cliff. And proper short courses at the college, run by farmers, so we can learn the new systems from people we trust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pigs themselves. A robot can count piglets, but I don't know if a robot will notice a sow that's just not herself today.

headlineQuote: A robot can count piglets, but I don't know if a robot will notice a sow that's just not herself today.
portrait: Carlos, 58, manages a **400-hectare farm** with an outdoor pig unit for two brothers.
He uses AI **now and then** and prefers to be the second one through the gate.
His standing worry is the **pig price**, which he has ridden out three times.
In fast scenarios he expects to **lose his desk** first, then his hands-on work at 63.
With more time he aims to **run the robots** and hand over cleanly to his stockman.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would make him a stockman at 60 and jobless at 63.
whatWouldHelp: A gentle **part-time step-down** with a top-up for older managers.
Short **college courses** run by farmers on the new systems.
